subject: chemistry
title: Structural and E/Z isomerism
key_idea: **Isomers** have the same molecular formula but different structures. **Structural isomers** differ in how the atoms are joined. **Stereoisomers** have the same structural formula but a different arrangement in space, as in E/Z isomerism around a C=C bond.

blocks.text: Structural isomers share a molecular formula but have different structural formulae. There are three kinds.

items.meaning: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
Different arrangements of the carbon skeleton, such as straight and branched chains.
The same carbon skeleton and functional group, with the group on different carbons.
The same atoms arranged as different functional groups.

diagram.alt: A sorting task: decide which kind of structural isomerism links each pair.
diagram.prompt: Sort each pair of isomers into the kind of structural isomerism.

blocks.text: Finding all the isomers of a formula

items.lead: Start with the longest straight chain.
Shorten the chain by one carbon
items.text: and place that carbon as a methyl branch on each different position. This gives 2-methylbutane.
Two methyl branches on a three-carbon chain gives 2,2-dimethylpropane.
A methyl group on an end carbon only makes a longer chain, so it is not a new isomer.

items: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.
The three kinds are chain, position and functional group.
Work through the isomers in order and watch for repeats.

blocks.text: Stereoisomers have the same structural formula but a different arrangement of atoms in space. E/Z isomerism is one kind, found in alkenes.

items.meaning: Compounds with the same structural formula but a different arrangement of atoms in space.
A type of stereoisomerism caused by restricted rotation about a C=C bond.
A special case of E/Z isomerism where two of the groups, one on each carbon of the C=C, are the same.

items: The C=C bond contains a **π bond**, so the two carbons cannot rotate about the bond.
The atoms attached to the C=C are fixed in one plane, so groups stay on the same side or on opposite sides.
E/Z isomerism needs **two different groups on each carbon** of the C=C.
But-2-ene has two forms. cis-but-2-ene has both CH₃ groups on the same side, and trans-but-2-ene has them on opposite sides.

items.lead: Look at one carbon of the C=C.
items.text: Give the two atoms attached to it a priority. The atom with the higher atomic number has the higher priority.

items.lead: If the first atoms are the same,
items.text: look at the atoms they are attached to, and compare them in the same way.
This gives a higher-priority group on each carbon.
Higher-priority groups on the same side give the **Z** isomer. Higher-priority groups on opposite sides give the **E** isomer.

items: Z comes from the German zusammen, meaning together. E comes from entgegen, meaning opposite.
E can be treated as trans and Z as cis only when each carbon of the C=C has a hydrogen atom.
In 1-bromo-2-chloroethene, bromine beats hydrogen on carbon 1 and chlorine beats hydrogen on carbon 2, so those are the priority groups.
E/Z isomerism comes from restricted rotation about a C=C bond.
Each carbon of the C=C must have two different groups.
Z: higher-priority groups on the same side. E: on opposite sides.

checks.q: Draw and name two chain isomers with the molecular formula C₄H₁₀.
Explain why but-2-ene shows E/Z isomerism but but-1-ene does not.
checks.a: The π bond in C=C stops rotation, and each carbon of the C=C in but-2-ene has two different groups (H and CH₃). In but-1-ene, one carbon of the C=C has two hydrogens, which are the same.

checks.q: State what makes the Z isomer different from the E isomer.
checks.a: In the Z isomer the two higher-priority groups (by CIP rules) are on the same side of the C=C. In the E isomer they are on opposite sides.

items: Given a molecular formula, work out possible structural formulae.
Given a structural formula, work out the possible E/Z or cis–trans stereoisomers.
Assigning CIP priorities to double or triple bonds within the R groups is not required.
Given a molecular formula, work out the possible structural, displayed and skeletal formulae.
Understand stereoisomerism using E/Z isomerism as the example, including cis–trans where two of the groups are the same.
Define the terms structural isomer and stereoisomer.
Draw the structures of chain, position and functional group isomers.
Draw structural formulae for the E and Z isomers.
Apply the CIP priority rules to decide which isomer is E and which is Z.

blocks.text: Stereoisomerism has two divisions: geometrical (cis/trans) and optical isomerism. E/Z naming may be used but is not required.

items: Explain the origin of cis/trans isomerism through restricted rotation due to the π bond.
Identify cis/trans isomerism in a molecule of given structural formula, including cyclic compounds.
Identify chiral centres in a molecule. A chiral centre is a carbon atom attached to four different groups.
Deduce the possible isomers of an organic molecule from its molecular formula.
Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images of each other, and they arise from a chiral centre.
In a ring, cis/trans isomerism arises because the ring stops rotation. Two carbons each carry two different groups, which sit on the same face or opposite faces of the ring.
